title: Gaggan Anand's Homecoming: The Rebel Chef Finally Opens in India
excerpt: Twenty years after leaving India, the two-Michelin-star chef has opened Raga in Delhi with longtime collaborator Rydo Anton — a full-circle moment for the man who once said the country wasn't ready for him.
body:
• Gaggan Anand — Asia's best restaurant five years running and a two-Michelin-star chef in Bangkok — has opened Raga, his first restaurant in India, at 21A Janpath Road in Delhi.
  • Raga is a partnership with Rydo Anton, the Indonesian-born chef who joined Anand's Bangkok kitchen in 2013; the name blends "Ra" and "Ga" with a nod to the Indian classical raga.
  • Anand, who once said India was "not ready" for his cooking, credits a new generation of young Indian chefs for giving him the confidence to return 20 years after leaving.
  • The 22-course Delhi menu marks a full-circle moment for the Kolkata-born chef, who nearly quit cooking in the capital 25 years ago after a frustrating early stint in its hotel kitchens.

The Prodigal Chef Comes Home

For two decades, Gaggan Anand built his legend everywhere but home. His Bangkok restaurant held the title of Asia's best restaurant five years in a row, earned two Michelin stars and sat in the top ten of the World's 50 Best Restaurants list — all while the Kolkata-born chef insisted India was not ready for what he cooks.

That has now changed. Raga, Anand's first restaurant in India, has opened its doors at 21A Janpath Road in Delhi, serving a 22-course menu built on the ingredient-and-technique experimentation that made him famous: the surprises, the humour, the dishes that ask diners to submit to the chef's rules.

He is not doing it alone. Raga is a partnership with Rydo Anton, the Indonesian-born chef who walked into Anand's Bangkok kitchen in 2013, waited four hours just for a trial, and worked his way up to head chef over more than a decade. Anton now leads the Delhi kitchen as an equal partner. The name reflects the pairing — "Ra" for Rydo Anton, "Ga" for Gaggan Anand — with a nod to the Indian classical raga, its structure and its space for improvisation.

Why Now

In an interview with India Today Spice, Anand was blunt about what changed his mind. "India, maybe 10 years or five years back, was not ready for me," he said, describing fine dining in India then as an uphill task. What gave him confidence, he said, was a new generation: "I must give credit to young generation of chefs, Varun, Prateek, Johnson, Hussain and Adwait, as they gave me confidence that I can do, all that I do abroad, now in India. These five chefs and their restaurants that are not in a hotel are pushing the envelope."

Anand has called 2026 a landmark year: beyond the India opening, he is renovating his Bangkok restaurant with a completely new experience — and banning phone photography in the dining room. Diners will not be allowed to click photos.

"India, maybe 10 years or five years back, was not ready for me. From the way I look at food, the way I present food, I felt fine dining was an uphill task in India."

— Gaggan Anand

The Fear He Had to Conquer

For Anand, Delhi is personal. In a 2023 interview with NDTV's Gargi Rawat, he recalled how, at 22, frustrated by long hours and an industry he found stifling, he rode his bike in circles outside a Delhi hotel in 2001 and went home thinking he would quit cooking altogether. "Your fear is your biggest challenge to overcome," he said of that moment.

He returned to Delhi for a 20-day residency in 2023 — deliberately a residency, not a pop-up — to test whether he could succeed in the capital. "A pop-up is not a sprint, it's a marathon," he explained at the time. "I wanted to overcome my fear that I would not do well in Delhi." Raga is the answer.

What It Means

Anand's return lands at a moment when Indian fine dining is arguably the most exciting it has ever been, with young chefs reworking regional cuisines and drawing global attention. His own journey — from nearly quitting in Delhi to redefining Indian food abroad, from resigning from his own restaurant with $3,000 in his pocket to the top of Asia's rankings — is now coming full circle.

For the diaspora, the symbolism is hard to miss: the chef who once said he became famous because he was away from India, who treasured his roots from a distance to reinvent them, is finally cooking at home. As he told diners years ago during a Taj pop-up tour: "Get ready for madness." Delhi is about to find out what he meant.
